children: Wall Street investment bankers just won a US election referendum. Democrats retaking control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in such convincing fashion will fuel expectations that they can reclaim the White House in two years. Logic follows that it would usher back an era of tougher trustbusting. The political calculus, and financial history, imply that CEOs will accelerate M&A activity.

Dealmakers anticipated, and then capitalized on, more accommodating reviews inside President Donald Trump’s Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission. The agencies concluded 16 significant merger investigations last year, one of the lowest tallies since 2011, with more quick settlements before trial and a sharp decline in abandoned transactions, according to law firm Dechert.
Ice purveyor Reddy Ice and industrial equipment manufacturer Columbus McKinnon
are among those that secured approval for deals by agreeing to divest certain businesses. Tractor maker Deere
and concert venue owner Live Nation
also signed anti-competition settlements that Joe Biden’s administration probably would not have approved.

His captains of competition, Lina Khan and Jonathan Kanter, took a much harder line, albeit with mixed success in court. They upended decades of antitrust convention, dusting off long-forgotten competition theories and rejecting mergers rather than blessing them with so-called behavioral remedies. A return to such a regime would thwart ambitious and chunky consolidation. The chances of a Democrat being elected president in 2028 have jumped to 66% on prediction market Kalshi from 53% a year ago.

Greater political clarity tends to sharpen financial minds. Although many economic and industry-specific factors go into corporate strategies, one similar scenario may be instructive. The last time a party lost both congressional chambers while occupying the Oval Office was 20 years ago. In the year that followed, US merger activity surged 32%, to $1.8 trillion, from the previous four quarters, according to LSEG data.

There are countervailing forces. For one thing, the $4.3 trillion of announced US transactions under Trump through September 2026 already represents a 65% increase from the previous seven quarters. China putting the kibosh this week on SoftBank's plan to buy ABB’s robotics division for $5.4 billion also provides a reminder of the stiffening resolve around the world. CEO confidence, an important spur for M&A, also is back on the wane, based on the Conference Board’s closely followed tracker.

Any boss mapping out the US political scene will have more to consider than just antitrust policy. Consumers are squeezed, business pricing power is weakening and it is easy to imagine the corporate tax rate going up if Democrats control both the executive and legislative branches. Acquiring rivals might be a way to shore up deteriorating margins. With profitability and antitrust pressure both on the ticket, expect boards to vote with their deal wallets.
Follow Jeffrey Goldfarb on X and Linkedin.

Democrats flipped control of both the US House of Representatives and Senate in midterm elections on November 3. With some races yet to be decided as of November 5, they have won 54 of the 100 Senate seats and 237 of 435 in the House, according to Reuters. Democrats also have added five governors nationwide, giving them 28 at the latest count.
